guess am still am) looking for a better solution on changing the card to
keep its original intent. We just use it a lot around here to bring out the
9s, 10s, and IC vamps. Just hate to see it go thats all.

Wish there was a way of turning it into something like this....
Tomb of Ramses III - master unique location. No cost.
Put on a vampire in your uncontrolled region. If the vamp's capacity is 10
or 11, then the vamp may be influenced for only 9 pool. If the vampire's

gives a nice ability (original intent).

> bleed action:" specifies "Prey".

Regarding that subject, I just found something of an inconsistency in
the Bleed Action cards regarding that new ruling vs the old ones and the
"motivation" behind them.

Most of them mention "(D)Bleed +X", and from previous interpretations,
that meant "Bleed any body you wish"; from the most recent one,
"(D)Bleed your prey", as the rules says.

Night Moves says "(D)Bleed your prey or your predator", so it explicitly
restrict the previous general ruling, or enhance the new ruling.

Kindred Spirits says "(D)Bleed any Meth", so it is redundant when
compared with the old rule, or an enhancement on the newest.

Speed of Though says "(D)Bleed your prey", so it restricts the previous
rule, or uselessly repeat the newest one.

Are there other cases I'm forgetting about?

Anyway. I just wanted to point these apparent "inconsistencies" to
everyone. It would seem that, even since the begining of the game, WotC
(and the RTR) doesn't really know what to make of (D)Bleed action
(because of the cards initially printed, or the rulings later made).
Seems like some errata will be required to get rid of the
"inconsistencies", or the useless repeating of basic rules (which cards
are "supposed to change", if they bring them up). :-)

Frederic.

Messages.Author: just...@my-dejanews.com
Messages.Body:
> These changes you've been making have been making have, although being
> drastic, been good - sometimes on closer inspection, but nevertheless.
> The idea of fixing powerful cards is a jolly good idea. However, in
> our local playing there has been one powerful card which hasn't been
> touched by the rulings. Now I know this card hasn't really gotten a lot
> of coverage on the newsgroup, not that I've noticed anyway, as being
> powerful but trust me it is, if you need an explanation just ask.

> That card is Hostile Takeover. And the reason why I'm mentioning
> this now, apart from being of the opinion that something should be
> done about it, is because a new rule makes it more powerful.
>

> > Golden Rule of Card Ownership [snipped]
>
> Now you can take someone's vampire, kill them and still have the
> vampire. The card is now more powerful - and it is the opinion of
> many in our playing group, including the person who uses it, that
> the card was already quite a powerful card.
>

Hostile Takeover is far from a safe card to use in the first place. I fail to
see why it should be modified since its effect is generally balanced. If you
bid for a vampire and subsequently gain it, the target Methusaleh gains a
generous amount of pool. This can also leave you in a precarious position if
you had to bid a large amount to gain control of the vampire. Therefore,
although you can possibly gain a large vampire, this is more than offset by
the fact that you have brought yourself considerably closer to being ousted
by giving a substantial amount of your pool to someone else.

Secondly, the vampires that are used by other Methusalehs are often quite
incompatible with those that I use. So if I name a vampire with a Hostile
Takeover, then the chances are it's going to be much less useful to me than my
own vampires.

Thirdly, why is there any need to change a card that there have been no
complaints about until now? I mean, if you are seriously worried about people
playing Hostile Takeover, then put some Sudden Reversals in your deck. A
couple of these should be enough to convince the Methusaleh playing them to
target someone else.

If cards like Hostile Takeover are going to be banned just because one person
has a problem with it, then maybe everybody should make changes for cards
they don't like. For instance, I don't like the fact that Arika got into
combat with Badger the other day, and Badger played 12 Drawing out the Beast,
and an Earth Meld. Net result, Arika went to torpor with no blood, and Badger
took no damage. Now, I'm not too happy about how easy it is to dump handfuls
of Drawing out the Beast, but that's the way it works so I guess I'll just
have to live with it. Instead, of spending time complaining about more cards
to fix, I think we should be working on trying to adapt to all the changes
that have already been made.

Anyway, maybe I'm biased because I spent lots of time resources collecting
Hostile Takeovers and I don't suddenly want to see them suddenly become next
to useless.

Later,

Billy.

Messages.Author: cbo...@apdi.net
Messages.Body:
> > This ruling
> > is a joke. It would be better to just ban the card along with RTI and TB.
> If Tomb is worthless then why should you care if anyone chooses to play
> with it in the future?

No, of course not. But I'd be kind of curious why they wasted their
pool (and their time).

Let's evaluate this new Tomb. (assuming you are in a position that
starts you out at 4 transfers)
To bring out a(n): - it costs (net loss/gain):

11 cap vampire -
3 Pool (ToR) + 8 Pool Transfers (2 turns) + 3 turns (for ToR effect) =
0 gain and 2 turns longer to bring vamp out

8 cap vampire -
3 pool (ToR) + 4 Pool Transfers + 4 turns (for ToR effect) =
1 gain and 3 turns longer to bring vamp out

6 cap vampire
3 Pool (ToR) + 3 Pool Transfers (so you don't lose any) + 3 turns =
0 gain and 2 turns longer to bring vamp out.

Of course, you can take longer to bring said vamp out to realize
more of a gain, but it can't be a vampire that you need. You can
also transfer more pool to gain speed, but then you are talking
about a net loss. So, effectivly, it is useless for it's intended
purpose - to influence out vampires. Unless, of course, you don't
mind waiting 6 or 8 or more turns to bring that vamp out.

So, what does that leave us with? To use it as a pool gainer, which,
if I recall correctly, was an even greater complaint as to the use
of the card than using it to influence out high cap vampires. Just
stick ToR on a vamp you know you won't influence out, tap to put a
blood on it and pull that blood back into your pool. Sweet.
IMO, this eratta does nothing to fix what most of you thought was
wrong with the card and at the same time turning it into wallpaper.

Sorrow

In most cases, I would agree. For example:

] Pander is a clan (while Caitiff still is not). [Sabbat]

] resolved at close range. [LSJ 970904]

I wouldn't exactly say that these are directly derivable from card
text, rules, or other errata. Maybe these are addressed in other
general rulings. The point is, you have to hunt around to find
clarification on your gut instinct. And with the number of errata
and rulings

178 of the 558 rulings/errata/clarification are clarifications.
That means 380 rulings and errata. The odds are really pretty good
(about 33%) that an ambiguous card or situation might be cleared up
by a ruling or errata. It'd be best just to include them all
together.

> As an aside:
> The elimination of the (D)-symbol non-reminder erratum also eliminates
> about 20 other errata (to Blood Bond, Blood Hunt, Cat Burglary, etc.)

Awesome! LSJ, I really respect you and what you are trying to do
with the game, and I hope none of my comments have been too harsh.
But they are based on the same feelings for this great game that you
use to try to correct some problems.

I just think that if you had gone about just fixing the old RT's
mistakes and thereby hopefully reducing the number of
errata/rulings/clarifications, people would probably have been more
receptive to your other card changes. By fixing the mistakes of
the past team, you would have been building trust and loyalty. The
way you've done it, people feel like you were just waiting to get the
RT power so you could make your house rules the real rules.

I beg of you that if you really want to earn people's respect and
loyalty, take back all the card specific rulings that deviate greatly
from card text and concentrate on reducing previous rulings and
errata to make the game less unwieldy. Once you've done that, people
will really feel you know what you are doing and be more than happy
to follow you as you try to improve the game.

Mike

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
Okay, I've read more or less everything on the group that I have at the
moment on the subject so now I'll through in my two-pence.

>New Rule:
>---------
>
>No vote pushing: Each Methuselah can only play no more than one

> Political Action card to gain a vote during a political action,
> including the Political Action card used to call the vote, if any.
> #
> # Idea: arguable reading of the original Jyhad rules. Fixes the
> # same problem that the DCI vote-replenishment rule attempted to
> # fix (so the DCI rule shouldn't be used with this rule).

No bad thing. It's still quite possible to get votes going - lots of
cards like Ventrue Headquarters, the Mausoleum, Ventrue Directorate
Assembly, Powerbase: Rome, Power Structure and so on can give you some
permanent votes and this might make such cards more useful. Limiting it
to permanent votes on vampires is also no bad thing as it will shift the
game back towards using higher capacity vampires which isn't bad in and
of itself.

>
>Other Changes to the Rules (or changes to Errata to the rules):
>---------------------------------------------------------------
>
>Golden Rule of Card Ownership has been modified. Your cards are still
> your own, but are not burned when you are ousted - only the cards
> that you control are burned when you are ousted. The rest (stolen
> by or traded to other players) are returned to you when they are
> burned or when the game ends.
>

Okay, I don't have a problem with this either. It helps make Corruption
a viable strategy because before you couldn't really steal your prey's
vamps because that would help you oust him (good thing) but then you'd
lose your vampires (bad thing).

>Directed actions are actions that directly affect another Methuselah,

> one of her minions, or a card a Methuselah controls. Cards that
> involve directed actions have a "(D)" in the card text. Nondirected
> actions are actions that are not directed against a Methuselah or one
> of her minions. Hunting, equipping a minion, recruiting an ally, and
> employing a retainer are examples of nondirected actions.

Hmmm.... I don't think I like this on face value. But Robert Goudie's
cries of "It stops people working out who's the biggest threat and then
ganging up on them" has kind of worked on me. ISTR reading an article
in the back of Duelist with Richard Garfield which mentioned a game he
played and it turning into simple diplomacy based on who held the
strongest territories or something. I think this helps stop Jyhad being
like that. However, I *do* know that it will have a big influence on
some decks which used bleed as a defence against their predator. Ho
hum.

>
>Equipment: is not optional, except as noted on card text. (Note: weapons
> always grant the ability to strike, but the minion is still free to
> use other strikes.)

Perhaps the wording should be cleared up to resolve the issues about
equipment which obviously IS optional - things like Leather Jacket which
you don't HAVE to burn.

>
>Aggravated Damage: aggravated damage done to a ready vampire sends the
> vampire to torpor (since it cannot be healed) but does not cause the
> vampire to burn any blood. Aggravated damage done to a vampire with
> unhealed damage (including aggravated damage after the first point)
> requires that the vampire burn one blood per point of damage to avoid
> being burned.
> #
> # Like the original Jyhad rules, only without the "packet" problems.
> # Some of the aggravated-damage-dealing effects from the original set
> # (and some from later sets) were unbalanced with the VTES-style
> # aggravated damage rules, so this serves to restore some of the balance
> # to those.
>

I think I prefer this a little. It's VERY complicated here and should
be re-written. The first sentence "but does not cause the vampire to
burn any blood" is very awkward when contrasted with the fact that it's
only the first point which isn't burned. But I like the clearing up of
the intent of the Jyhad rules - it was always difficult to know if
vampires were burned because of the fact that, say, the aggravated
damage from my claws and the aggravated damage from, say, my Pulled
Fangs were resolving at different times so was my vampire burned or not
(argue ad nauseum).

>CARDS:
>
>Darius Styx:
> "Non-Camarilla. As an action, Darius may allow his controller to look at one
> card at random from any other Methuselah's hand. If it is an equipment card
> or a retainer card, it is placed on Darius at no cost."

Fine. Limits the card to what it was supposed to do.

>
>Fame:
> "Unique Master. Put this card on a ready vampire. If the vampire with this
> card goes to torpor, then his controller burns 3 pool. Each Methuselah
> burns 1 pool during his or her untap phase if this vampire is in torpor."

No, I don't like this. Either way, it's still abusable simply because
of it's repeat capacity during a turn. I don't mind it being used
OFFENSIVELY (ie I do damage to YOUR vamps and you lose pool) since it
does bolster the beleaguered combat decks a little but I still think its
difficult with it being used more than once in a turn. Maybe:

"The first time the vampire with this card goes to torpor since your
(the controller who plays this card) untap phase, then this vampire's
controller burns three pool."

Whatever, I just don't think it should be usable repeatedly during
turns. The thing about the untap phase was based on the fact that
CI/Madness Network would get round it.

>
>Fire Dance:
> Is directed or not based on the controller of the target, as always.
> #

Fine.

>Goth Band:
> "As a +1 stealth (D) action, the Goth Band may move one counter from
> a master card controlled by another Methuselah to a master card you
> control that uses counters."

Fine.

>Heidelburg Castle, Germany:
> Cannot be used during an action (including during a combat, since that
> is part of the action now - including combats resulting from blocks).
> Can be used after an action resolves and before the next action begins, at
> the beginning of any minion phase, or at any time outside of the minion
> phase.

The "or at any time outside of the minion phase" might conflict with the
Play-Resolve thing. I play a card to put a card I own up for sale, say,
Malkavian Time Auction and I choose a vamp with Sengir Dagger on it.
During the bidding, I tap Heidelberg to move the Sengir Dagger off it.
I can hear the arguments now:

"But you can't interrupt the resolution."
"But the card says at any time!"

<whine ad infinitum>

>
>Major Boon:
> "Play this card when another Methuselah is successfully bled. Not usable if
> you control the acting minion. The bleed amount may be modified after this
> card is played. You burn pool for the bleed instead of the target Methuselah
> (must be at least 1 pool) and give this card to the target Methuselah. You
> may burn this card to have that Methuselah burn pool instead of you when you
> are successfully bled."
> #
> # The VTES version munged the "may be modified" clause pretty badly
>

I see the need for this alteration based on things like Madness Network
and Anson. Bleed your prey for fuck loads outside of his turn and
there's very little he can do to stop you playing this, especially if
it's down to only two people cos he can't plead for an SR off anyone
else.

>Mind Rape:
> "Superior: (D) put this card on a younger vampire and tap that vampire.
> The vampire with this card does not untap as normal during his
> controller's untap phase. During the acting vampire's controller's next
> minion phase, she must burn this card to untap the vampire and take
> control of the vampire until the end of her turn."

Hmmm... not too bad.

>
>Of Noble Blood:
> Is directed or not based on the controller of the target (and the
> definition of "directed").
>

Fine.

>Powerbase: Mexico City
> The action to steal the blood from your powerbase cannot be attempted
> by your own vampires.
>

Fine.

>Pulled Fangs:
> The damage is not aggravated.
> #
> # to balance the card with Lucky Blow, Disarm, and Twisting the Knife.
>

I don't agree with this one. Pulled Fangs can now be more easily
prevented due to things like Skin of Rock being playable against it.
Maybe just make it unable to burn you. So, maybe just send the vampire
to torpor.

>Return to Innocence:
> Action - 4 blood.
> Bleed. If you successfully bleed your Prey for one or more, put this card
> on the acting vampire. Burn this card if this vampire loses any blood or
> goes to torpor, or if your Prey is ousted. During your next untap, this
> vampire is removed from play and your Prey burns X pool, where X is the
> capacity of this vampire.
> #
> # to offset the "sudden death" aspect somewhat - not sure if it goes far
> # enough, though. We'll see.

It works weirdly. I don't think it will work too well. I'd have to see
it tried first. But it looks like it may well just be ban material
simply because the idea of a +X bleed is simply broken.

>
>Sleeping Mind:
> Cards played after Sleeping Mind are still free to break these rules, as
> always. So while you are provented from untapping (with Rat's Warning),
> for instance, you are not prevented from playing Wake to block - since
> Wake allows you to attempt to block "as if untapped", and untapped
> vampires can still block the action as normal.

I don't know if I like this now. It's difficult to judge it, I guess.

>
>Thoughts Betrayed:
> "Superior: Opposing minion cannot play strike cards for the rest of combat."

There is the problem, though, that I feel it was created to help the
Tremere get to second round. Maybe do something like:

"Superior: Opposing minion cannot play maneuver cards/strike cards/press
cards (choose one) for the remainder of combat."

>
>Tomb of Ramses III:
> "Master: Unique Location. 3 pool.
> When this card is brought into play, or the controller of this card changes,
> the controller chooses a vampire in her uncontrolled region. During your
> influence phase, tap to move 1 blood from the blood bank to the chosen
> vampire. Burn this card when the chosen vampire leaves the uncontrolled
> region
.

No, I don't like this one at all. As I see it, the card was originally
intended to let you get out a big vampire quickly, to trouble the weenie
decks. So my suggestion would be:

"When this card is brought....... uncontrolled region <verbatim>. At
the end of your influence phase, if the chosen vampire has blood equal
to or greater than half their capacity, move them to the controlled
region and give them enough blood to reach capacity from the blood bank,
and burn this card."

>Treatment, The:
> The action to burn this card is directed (unless the Prince and the
> Treatment somehow come to be controlled by the same Methuselah), by the
> definition of a directed action.
>

Fine.

>Wake with Evening's Freshness:
> "Do not replace until your next untap phase."
>

Unnecessary. I know that LSJ's group plays with all sorts of
restrictions on wakes but I don't think this is necessary. Wakes are
not a "no brain" choice for a deck - maybe desirable but not necessarily
necessary. I think it's fine as is, myself.

>Zip Gun:
> Cannot use ammo cards.
>

I dunno. It does kind of rip the guts out of the card. Maybe make it
pay to use ammo cards, instead? After all, DBR for a Zip Gun would be a
mite expensive, surely?

Messages.Author: mboh...@my-dejanews.com

In article <35A660E6...@lmco.com>,
michae...@lmco.com wrote:

> TOR is better when
> 1) Playing a clan with no ET equivelent or want more.
> 2) You can afford to leave a vampire uninfluenced.

Look at it this way:

You pay 3 pool. What do you get for that 3 pool? One free blood
for influence each turn until the vampire it is on comes into play.
Let's assume you are using it to bring out a vampire.

Turn Action Total Cost Recouped
1 Play ToR, Use ToR, Use 4 Transfers 1 Pool
2 Use ToR, Use (Capacity-6) Transfers 2 Pool

At this point, a vampire of capacity 10 or less comes into play.
So you must ask yourself, is it worth paying one pool to get a
vampire out one turn faster (if it's a 9 or 10 capacity)?

Considering that Information Superhighway is permanent, costs
nothing, and has the same effect (plus 2 more transfers) I would
say no.

The ONLY situation where you would reasonably use ToR is if you are
bringing out an Inner Circle Member (you'll recoup your third pool,
but it still took you just as long to bring it out as
normal - 3 turns) or you are using it for pool gain. Quite frankly
there are better pool gainers that are more reliable.

Conclusion - Nearly wallpaper. To be honest, I didn't think that
this change was that bad, but now that I've sat down and put down
the numbers, it's terrible.

Mike Bohlmann

Chris Berger wrote:

> > etc.)

> Yes, but your insistence that it somehow makes bleeds only directable
> at prey adds about 20 more errata. (Every card that says "(D)
> Bleed..." must say "(D) Bleed your prey...")

That's not true. Here's the argument, step by step; if you disagree
with any of the steps, let me know.

1. Without a specific card, you may only bleed your prey.
2. The new rule says that a (D) action does not automatically provide
omni-directability.
3. A card which says "(D) Bleed" allows you to use this card (presumably
with some added benefit) to perform the natural bleed action, i.e.,
against your prey.

Hence, for you to be able to bleed someone other than your prey, you
have to have a card which specifically lets you. The only reason there
were cards printed that say "(D) Bleed your prey" is because those were
printed under the (now overturned) (D)-omni-directability rule.

> That's not true. Here's the argument, step by step; if you disagree

> 1. Without a specific card, you may only bleed your prey.
> 2. The new rule says that a (D) action does not automatically provide

>
> Hence, for you to be able to bleed someone other than your prey, you
> have to have a card which specifically lets you. The only reason there
> were cards printed that say "(D) Bleed your prey" is because those were
> printed under the (now overturned) (D)-omni-directability rule.
>

Okay. I follow your reasoning. I don't, however, agree with your
logic.

1. A bleed action is not *defined* as only being able to affect any
particular methuselah.
2. The default (cardless) bleeding action restricts you to only being
able to affect your prey.
3. A card which allows you to bleed has two options: a) Specifically
restrict you to bleeding a particular methuselah (your prey), or b) Just
plain allow you to "bleed."
4. Cross-reference 3 with 1.

The word "bleed" doesn't restrict you to bleeding your prey. Therefore,
all cards that you want to work that way must be errata'd.

-Chris

Messages.Author: Gomi no Sensei
Messages.Body:
In article <35A70E3...@cco.caltech.edu>,
Chris Berger <ber...@cco.caltech.edu> wrote:

>Okay. I follow your reasoning. I don't, however, agree with your
>logic.

Logic, more or less definitionally, is irrelevant to 'agreement.'
You may disagree with the *premises* the logic is derived from, but
if you 'follow the reasoning,' you have implicitly agreed with the
logic.

>1. A bleed action is not *defined* as only being able to affect any
>particular methuselah.

This is incorrect. Section 6.4 of the rulebook explicitly uses 'prey'
in the definition of the 'bleed' action. Specific cardtext is required
to override this definition.

v.g.:

"6.4. Minion Actions

[...]

Bleed (no card required):

[...]

To have one of your minions commit a bleed action:

1) Tap the minion and announce to your prey that your minion is attempting
to bleed.
2) If your prey's minions cannot block, or are unsuccessful in their
attempts to stop you, your prey burns one pool."

Action cards that state 'bleed' can only be directed at your prey, by
definition of 'bleed,' barring specific cardtext to the contrary. QED.

>2. The default (cardless) bleeding action restricts you to only being
>able to affect your prey.

Per the definition of 'bleed,' above.

>3. A card which allows you to bleed has two options: a) Specifically
>restrict you to bleeding a particular methuselah (your prey), or b) Just
>plain allow you to "bleed."

3(b) is inclusive of, and equivalent to, 3(a) with the parenthetized (your
prey) clause. A third option (3(c)) is required to allow bleeds of other,
non-prey Metheuselahs.

>The word "bleed" doesn't restrict you to bleeding your prey. Therefore,
>all cards that you want to work that way must be errata'd.

'Bleed,' by definition, restricts the valid target of the action to one's
prey, and specific cardtext is required to override that.

gomi

Messages.Author: Elliott
Messages.Body:
These new changes suck! They are much to difficult to remember and
totaly disrupt the original intent of the card. I agree that when some
clever player finds a way to abuse a card so much as to make it
overpowered it should be changed. However, I feel it is VERY important
to maintain the original, INTENDED purpose of the card. I have included
a couple of relevant examples.

Tomb of Ramses was never intended to be a way to draw infinite pool, it
was supposed to be a way to get a large vamp out quicker. Here is my
simple interpretation/change:

Put this card on a vamp in your uncontrolled region. For each blood
counter you transfer to THIS vampire during your influence phase, move
one counter from the blood bank to this vamp. ADDITIONALLY, you may not
transfer blood counters FROM this vamp to your pool during your
influence phase. Burn this card when this vamp comes into play.

What about Fame? It was designed to protect your vamp, right? How easy
is this:

Put this card on a ready vamp YOU CONTROL. If the vamp is sent to torpor
by ANOTHER METHUSELAH OR HIS MINIONS, THAT Methuselah loses 3 pool. Each
Methuselah loses 1 pool during his or her untap phase as long as the
vamp is in torpor.

Don't these simple changes make a whole lot more sense, while still
preserving the original intent of the card? Please enlighten me on how
they could still be abused. I would also love to hear your ideas on some
of the other card changes that could have been done better.

Messages.Body:
Elliott wrote:
>
> These new changes suck! They are much to difficult to remember

Come on now. I know a lot of people have issues with the new rulings,
and one main (and certainly valid) complaint is that the game is harder
for new people to learn with lots of eratta. But how many cards have
been significantly changed? Less than 20, I think. The people who have
already memorized the existing changes to cards will, I think, have no
trouble remembering these new changes.

> and
> totaly disrupt the original intent of the card.

In the cases where the card was totally busted, I don't think this was
unwarranted. It is arguable that the intent of cards like ToRIII and
the like was "to bust the game". Such intent cannot be preserved.

> I agree that when some
> clever player finds a way to abuse a card so much as to make it
> overpowered it should be changed.

Players do not make the cards overpowered. The cards are themselves
overpowered. We do not advocate changing cards because people have
found a cool combo to use them in. We advocate changing cards because
they are busted.

> Tomb of Ramses was never intended to be a way to draw infinite pool,
> it was supposed to be a way to get a large vamp out quicker.

How do you know that? It certainly can be used as a pool gain card, so
how do you know that that was not its original intent. That may be how
you mainly used it, but who can say what was in the minds of the design
team?

> What about Fame? It was designed to protect your vamp, right? How easy
> is this:

If you say so. I think it was designed to simulate a vampire becoming
famous, and the effect the torporization of that vampire would have on
the table. Just watch the news for a couple of days and you'll see that
celebrities are not protected by their fame, but threatened by it. I
think LSJ's fix not only takes the brokenness of the card away, but also
captures this feeling nicely.

> Don't these simple changes make a whole lot more sense, while still
> preserving the original intent of the card?

These changes look exactly like others which have been posted here in
the five (!) days since the recent rulings. I don't really see why
these are preferable over LSJ's or over banning.

By the way, why are you so sure that people will universally accept your
changes when almost everyone has been decrying LSJ's? I think it was
Robert Goudie who expressed this best, but people are rigid animals.
Most of us are upset that LSJ made these changes without consulting us,
and this bothers us because _our_ changes are better, etc. So, I say
again, is it not better to just ban the broken card?

> As a methuselah of very little brain i don't really understand the concept
> of brokenness. One definition i saw was that a card is broken if you HAVE
> to put it in your deck. When i was building my combat deck i realised that
> Fame was that card - because i kept getting killed by it in real life, and

> main reason for Fame was to contest it if some other unscrupulous fellow
> played it .. and then i realised that i could KILL people with it too!!!!
>

You might be a broken card if:

1) Every (or almost every) deck requires the card. Any (or almost any) deck
that does not have this card is less effective than the same deck with this
card. (Ex: Tomb of Ramses III. Under old rules, basically any deck can add
in a Tomb (perhaps in place of an Art Museum or whatever) and it will be
better.)

2) The card is flat-out better than any similar cards. A card is "better"
than another if for all (or almost all) situations, this card may be
substituted for the other card and give equal effect AND: a) there are some
(or all) situations where this card gives better effects than the other card
b) there are some situations where this card can be used and the other cannot
(Ex: If there were a Master Card that said "Gain 2 pool from the blood bank,"
it would be broken because it is obviously better than Ascendance in all
situations and obviously better than StI in almost all situations.) Note:
This rule may sometimes be broken if the original card was so useless that it
would never be played anyway, and is regarded by the manufacturing company as
a mistake.

3) Using this one card (or possibly a very-small combo involving this card)
will ruin the chances of any deck that is not specifically designed to defeat
it, or which does not contain one or more of a relatively small class of
cards. (Ex: Return to Innocence. Under old rules, unless you use bleed
bounce or Archon Investigation, RtI is an "instant win" card.)

4) Using this one card alone will destroy a large class of decks. Thus simply
adding a few to your deck will literally win the game against anyone who plays
those decks.
(Ex: If there were a card which said: "You may not be bled while you have
minions in play," the card would be broken because it completely hoses bleed
decks, nominally 1/3 of basic deck archetypes. Archon Investigation borders
very closely on this.)

5) The word "Broken" appears in the title or trait text of the card. (Sorry,
joke from L5R... "Broken Sword of the Scorpion" and "Dragon Sword is Broken"
are often reffered to as "broken cards.")

-Chris

Rotz was reinterpreted to mean what it says.

Text:

Play when a minion attempts to use aggravated damage against a vampire,
whether successfully or not. Combat ends before damage is resolved. That
vampire is put in torpor, tapped, with this card on it. During the
vampire's next untap phase, burn this card instead of untapping the

Brujah with the perfect combination attempts to bleed. Little Ricki blocks.
Brujah plays Torn Signpost, Fists of Death, and Undead Strength to
really wail on poor Ricki. He is sitting there with a Sideslip and a Blur

and the Brujah starts to panic. Combat ends. No damage is done. Mr.
Brujah goes to topor. Poor Mr. Brujah can't even play his Sudden Reversal
since it is his turn. Rotsreich also beats out S:CE.

The new improved interpretation of Rotsreich just made aggravated damage
MUCH more effective and difficult to avoid the consequences of.

Messages.Author: Bernie Bresnahan
Messages.Body:
In the spirit of slight changes opposed to complete re-writes,
I submit the following on our old friend "Fame".

The original text (Jyhad):
FAME: Put this card on a ready Vampire.
If the Vampire goes to Torpor, the prey of the vampire loses 3 pool.
Each Methuselah loses 1 pool during his/her untap phase as
long as the Vampire is in Torpor

==== Possible Errata instead of Re-Writes ====

FAME: Put this card on a ready Vampire.
If the Vampire goes to Torpor, the prey of the vampire loses 3 pool.
THIS Methuselah loses 1 pool during his/her untap phase as
long as the Vampire is in Torpor

FAME: Put this card on a ready Vampire.
If the Vampire goes to Torpor, the prey of the vampire loses 3 pool.
Each Methuselah loses 1 pool during THE CONTROLLERS untap phase as
long as the Vampire is in Torpor

FAME: Put this card on a ready Vampire NOT YOUR OWN.
If the Vampire goes to Torpor, the prey of the vampire loses 3 pool.
Each Methuselah loses 1 pool during his/her untap phase as
long as the Vampire is in Torpor

=======================================
Whether ya'll like it or not, this is the kind of change I like to
see. Slight changes are much easier to introduce, rather than
complete re-writes..

Bernie Bresnahan

Cards are not broken.

1) I have never required a specific card to win or be successsful. To include
RtIII. Numerous extremely sucessful decks do not include "broken" cards. Burn the
location, sudden reversal, etc

2) Just because a card performs a function more succesfully than another card
does not indicate a roken state, it indicates a differing power level. Not all
cards were meant to be "equal", nor should they be.

3) RtI is powerful but there are a number of ways to counter this card. Design
a deck with some depth of strategy. A rush deck with no intercept will pay the
price for its lack of flexibility. I personally will exploit a persons lack of
forethought in deck design.

4) Archon investigation is a rough card but unless your deck is specifically
designed to be stealth bleed deck (again lack of forethought if thats all your
deck can do) , the loss of a vampire should not be debilitating. I include sudden
reversals for things such as this (political leverage for other meth turns).

I cannot stress this enough, build your decks with as much flexibilty a psossible
considering your deck concept a local playing enviroment.

-C

In article <35A282...@wizards.com>,

> No vote pushing: Each Methuselah can only play no more than one

I like this rule although it would be better if the
acting Methusaleh could push with one vote as
well (this interpretation is also supported by the
original rules, in addition to as the one proposed

>

I'm not quite sure why this rule was added.
Although it does add interesting possibilities for
stealing peoples vampires, locations, etc, it also
creates a big pain-in-the-ass for people who had
planned to do something else if they died early.
Maybe this should be a tournament-only rule,
when players are pretty much guaranteed to be
hanging around until the end of the game.

>
> Directed actions are actions that directly affect another Methuselah,
> one of her minions, or a card a Methuselah controls. Cards that
> involve directed actions have a "(D)" in the card text. Nondirected
> actions are actions that are not directed against a Methuselah or one
> of her minions. Hunting, equipping a minion, recruiting an ally, and
> employing a retainer are examples of nondirected actions.

Does this mean you can now play Temptation on
your own vampires?

> Equipment: is not optional, except as noted on card text.

This rule seems fine.

> Aggravated Damage: aggravated damage done to a ready vampire sends the
> vampire to torpor (since it cannot be healed) but does not cause the
> vampire to burn any blood. Aggravated damage done to a vampire with
> unhealed damage (including aggravated damage after the first point)

> being burned.

What were the "packet" problems associated with
the jyhad rules for aggro damage?
Anyway, doesn't this ruling make aggro damage
less powerful, and thereby further weaken
combat decks?
Won't this detract even further from the
competitiveness of combat decks?

> CARDS:
>
> Darius Styx:
> Goth Band:
> Fire Dance
> Of Noble Blood:
> Powerbase: Mexico City
> Treatment, The:

All these look fine.

>
> Fame:
> "Unique Master. Put this card on a ready vampire. If the vampire with this
> card goes to torpor, then his controller burns 3 pool. Each Methuselah
> burns 1 pool during his or her untap phase if this vampire is in torpor."

Yeah, I guess this removes the abuse aspect from
the card, while still allowing it to be useful in
other ways.

> Heidelburg Castle, Germany:
> Cannot be used during an action (including during a combat, since that
> is part of the action now - including combats resulting from blocks).
> Can be used after an action resolves and before the next action begins, at
> the beginning of any minion phase, or at any time outside of the minion

Is the second sentence really necessary?

>
> Major Boon:

Fine.

> Mind Rape:
> "Superior: (D) put this card on a younger vampire and tap that vampire.
> The vampire with this card does not untap as normal during his
> controller's untap phase. During the acting vampire's controller's next
> minion phase, she must burn this card to untap the vampire and take
> control of the vampire until the end of her turn."

Yikes. Now I think this is going just a bit too far
from the original wording and intent of the card. I
personally haven't had too much trouble with the
card, certainly not enough to warrant this sort of
card text change. If it really is such a problem,
maybe it should be just banned from tournament
play altogether.

>
> Pulled Fangs:
> The damage is not aggravated.

Yeeouch. This removes one of the main sources of
aggro damage for decks that do not contain
Thaumaturgy, Protean, or Quietus. Once again,
this seems to be to the detriment of combat decks
that don't contain the aforementioned disciplines.
Perhaps a different sort of ruling could be used.
For example, say that: each Pulled Fangs resolves
individually , such that the first Pulled Fangs
sends the vampire to torpor and prevents the
playing of subsequent pulled fangs. This also
implicitly requires the ruling that going to torpor
ends combat immediately, and that no more cards
can be played except for those with specific card-
text that are played when a vampire is going to

against

Strangely enough, I am more than happy with this
ruling. It brings it in line with other cards such

> When this card is brought into play, or the controller of this card changes,

No way. That's just ridiculous. The original intent
of the card is almost destroyed entirely, and the
card text is mangled beyond belief. How about this
change that preserves card text (pretty much)
and intent:

Tomb of Rameses
Master
Cost: 3
Master: unique location Put this card on a
vampire in your uncontrolled region. For each
blood counter you transfer to [this] uncontrolled

vampire during your influence phase, move one

counter from the blood bank to this vampire.
Burn this card when this vampire comes into
play.

This only requires the change of one word, whilst
still restricting the usefulness of the card for
bringing out multiple large vampires
simultaneously.
>
> Wake with Evening's Freshness:
> "Do not replace until your next untap phase."
>

Ugh. I've never had enough problems with Wake to
warrant this sort of ruling. Why is this change

untap phase.
Besides, the vote-pushing replacement was only
ever until the end of your minion/discard

because you wanted to _try_ (no guarantee of
success) to stop a few of your prey's actions.

> Zip Gun:
> Cannot use ammo cards.
>

I guess I reluctantly agree with this ruling.

Justicar.

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
Christopher Chew (c...@id4.telecom.fedex.com) wrote:
: Cards are not broken.

Others have already disputed this point, but I'm planning to do it in
my own particular idiom. ;-)

: 2) Just because a card performs a function more succesfully than another card

: does not indicate a roken state, it indicates a differing power level. Not all
: cards were meant to be "equal", nor should they be.

This, I think, is where our opinions begin to diverge, and why you reach
completely different conclusions from me (and some other people). My
idea of a good card game includes that it should embrace the principle
of balance in card design. That is, there should *not* be cards that
perform their functions better than other comparable cards. There
shouldn't *be* differing power levels among cards. My stance is that
all cards *are* meant to be equal, and should be. (It's probably
impractical for all cards to be exactly equal in 'power', so I'm
willing to settle for their being at least not blatantly out of line
with each other, which I think is the case for the others arguing in
favor of balance as well.)

It's fine, for example, to have Undead Strength and then Growing Fury -
the 2nd round or later restriction on GF makes its otherwise identical
cost (in terms of space in hand, in deck, blood cost to play, etc)
balanced with the 1 greater damage it does at each level. It's even
acceptable to also have Pushing the Limit and Lucky Blow - PtL costs
an additional blood to get the same bonus as GF, and Lucky Blow works
like inferior Undead Strength, but requires no discipline, and so pays
the cost of being a 'do not replace' card. All these reflect principles
of balance in card design.

But now look at Pulled Fangs versus, say, Twisting the Knife. Pulled
Fangs does 1 agg damage if the user inflicted more damage at close
range (under the old rules). Twisting the Knife does 1 regular damage
if the user did at least 3 damage with a hand or melee weapon, requires
Potence, costs 1 blood (PF costs 0 blood and requires no discipline).
The only apparent benefit is that TtK provides an optional press at
superior. These cards are not well balanced. Pulled Fangs is so much
better than TtK that no one would even consider using TtK over PF if
they had the choice. In my opinion, it's an indication of bad design
work that TtK was printed as it was. (PF was also somewhat overpowered
in relation to other comparable combat cards, but TtK is worse than
them as well - my argument here is not that PF was too powerful but
that TtK was not powerful enough.)

: 3) RtI is powerful but there are a number of ways to counter this card. Design

: a deck with some depth of strategy. A rush deck with no intercept will pay the
: price for its lack of flexibility. I personally will exploit a persons lack of
: forethought in deck design.

It is also my opinion that the existence of countermeasures is never
justification for an overpowered effect. The classic "action: oust
your prey" is a good example of this. It can be blocked, or Direct
Interventioned, but that doesn't make it balanced.

Josh

spreading the gospel of enlightened card design

Messages.Author: Alan Flesch
Messages.Body:
Pre-script. Stupid mailer. 'Replied via mail' rather
'Replied via newsgroup. Damn.

-----------------------

I had resolved to keep away from the 'rewrite' issues,
but this solution popped into my head, and I was powerless
to resist typing it in. :)

Not that I expect this version to fly, either...

Tomb of Rameses III Master 3 pool
UNIQUE LOCATION. Put this card on a vampire in your uncontrolled region.
For each blood counter you transfer to an uncontrolled vampire during
your influence phase, place one Tomb counter on to this
vampire. Treat Tomb counters as blood for the purpose of bringing
this vampire into play. Burn this card and all Tomb counters when
the vampire enters play.

Fixes proposed by this wording :

1) Big vampires can enter play quickly; they are not at full capacity,
but that's the penalty for bringing them into play ear

2) There is little 'pool cycling' going on; you can transfer blood back
and forth to the card, but the net effect is zero on your pool and
a big, empty vampire when it enters play.

3) If the Tomb moves, the Tomb counters remain functional for the purpose
of bringing vamps into play.

4) The counters are on the vamp (rather than the Tomb) to avoid problems
with Goth Bands.

5) It preserves the _intent_ of the card without changing a majority
of text.

Problems proposed by this wording

1) It introduces a penalty for play of the card - the vamp is no longer
at full capacity when it enters play.

2) Can be confusing to explain to new players.

Alan (aj)

> > and an Earth Meld. Net result, Arika went to torpor with no blood, and Badger

>
> > Now, I'm not too happy about how easy it is to dump handfuls
> > of Drawing out the Beast, but that's the way it works so I guess I'll just
> > have to live with it.
>
> So why cant people have lived with Tomb, Return, Rutor's Hand and all
> the rest of it?

Because LSJ and his rules-team determined that those cards were _broken_ as
they previously existed and needed to be fixed (except for Rutor's Hand which
was changed to remove an anomalous ruling about damage prevention outside of
combat). If you're not quite sure how to do determine whether a card is
broken or not then take a lot as this definition put forward by James
Hamblin:

"bro'ken (adj) : 1. Any card which costs less than, or has a more potent
effect than other comparable cards. 2. Any _single_ card which requires
concerted efforts from other players to thwart. 3. Any card which
prevents other players from playing the game."

Let's analyse Hostile Takeover with regard to these three points.

1.

Hostile Takeover ---------------- Requires a master action. Costs 1. Requires
a ready Ventrue. If another Methusaleh wins the auction, the previous owner
gains pool in exchange. If the controlling Methusaleh wins, they only pay
half the winning bid (rounded down).

Temptation of Greater Power --------------------------- Requires a master
action. Costs 3. Requires a ready Justicar. If another Methusaleh wins the
auction, the previous owner gains nothing. If the controlling Methusaleh
wins, they pay the whole amount of the winning bid (with the option of paying
some of it back later).

Now, I admit that Ventrue can be easier to get than Justicars, and that
Temptation of Greater Power (TGP) costs two pool more than Hostile Takeover
(HT), but TGP has a much more powerful effect. Assuming a winning bid of 10
pool by another Methuselah, the original owner would gain 10 pool in
compensation after a HT, and 0 pool after a TGP.

2. The Methusaleh of the chosen vampire receives pool in exchange for their
vampire so there is no need for other players to get involved (unless they
want the vampire themselves).

3. The Methusaleh is not prevented from doing anything. The auction is an
open process, open to all players. If someone thinks the current bid is too
low, then they can just bid higher. If they lose their vampire, then they
gain pool which allows them to bring out other vampires, or play pool-costing
cards that they previously couldn't afford.

>
> > Instead, of spending time complaining about more cards
> > to fix, I think we should be working on trying to adapt to all the changes
> > that have already been made.
>
> Yeah, there's logic. Better to stop half way to let everybody to catch up -
> and one they've caught up maybe change some other things.

Do I detect a note of sarcasm there? Maybe you should tell LSJ that you think
he's only gotten half-way and that he should be concentrating on making a lot
more changes, rather than checking to see that the current ones are OK.
Besides, if you think that there are more changes to be made, why don't you
suggest some yourself, rather than simply whining about things?

>
> > Anyway, maybe I'm biased because I spent lots of time resources collecting
> > Hostile Takeovers and I don't suddenly want to see them suddenly become next
> > to useless.
>
> Good to see you've got a bias. I'm biased as well I've collected a lot of
> HTs as well - it's because they were always a bloody awesome card and now
> they're even better. Hang on, if I'm biased that way why the heck am I
> speaking out against it - because it's wrong that's why.

As LSJ consistently points out, _wrong_ is simply a matter of opinion.
Personally, I can't see anything wrong with the card at all.
>
> So why were you spending resources to collect them? Maybe you just liked the
> artwork?

I've spent a lot of time and resources collecting Freak Drives, Kiss of Ra,
and Temptaion of Greater Power because I think they're bloody awesome cards.
Are you suggesting that just because people like to play a particular card
then it should be changed? Now there's some warped logic.

>
> I'm not trying to be agressive, I just don't agree with your stance and
> especially not with the logic you've used to get there.

Fair enough. Maybe you could suggest a way the card could be changed then,
rather than just making vague moanings and complainings, and hoping that
someone else will do it for you.

Justicar.

"don't do that to me, I'll come beat you up". But you'd do that anyway,
_probably_ with the vampire they're going to steal!

> and you can't
> think of something to do with the pool that you would gain in exchange for
> your vampire, then put in some Sudden Reversals to ease your mind.

Again, a deck which takes optimum advantage of this card would make sure
that you don't have a lot of pool to bid with. And if a card is so good
that you need Sudden Reversals to counter it, it's probably broken.

> Personally, I don't use Sudden Reversals to defend my vampires from Hostile
> Takeover. I usually find that a bit of creative diplomacy is enough to make
> people change their minds.

Unfortunately, a lot of people don't listen to diplomacy, even when it's
in their best interest. I found this a lot at Origins. There was a
weenie vote push deck at the table. It was having trouble, and was
pleading with the other people who had votes to help him out. And they
did! I was dumbfounded.

> If you're not quite sure how to do determine whether a card is
> broken or not then take a lot as this definition put forward by James
> Hamblin:

Heh. I'm so proud...

> "bro'ken (adj) : 1. Any card which costs less than, or has a more potent
> effect than other comparable cards. 2. Any _single_ card which requires
> concerted efforts from other players to thwart. 3. Any card which
> prevents other players from playing the game."
>
> Let's analyse Hostile Takeover with regard to these three points.
>

> Hostile Takeover ---------------- Requires a master action. Costs 1. Requires
> a ready Ventrue. If another Methusaleh wins the auction, the previous owner
> gains pool in exchange. If the controlling Methusaleh wins, they only pay
> half the winning bid (rounded down).

Actually, I would say that Hostile Takeover is borderline broken by my
definition.
By (2) the card is broken since it requires either a Sudden Reversal, or
a large expenditure of pool. By (3) the card is broken because it takes
away your vampire, thus reducing your ability to play the game.

[snip Tempation of Greater Power -- same problem]

> 2. The Methusaleh of the chosen vampire receives pool in exchange for their
> vampire so there is no need for other players to get involved (unless they
> want the vampire themselves).

Exactly. So it all comes down to how much pool the person who plays the
HT is willing to pay. And even if the deck isn't optimized for this
card, HT still very often ends up being a master-phase-bleed-for-four.
What other master cards cause a directed pool loss, and how do they
compare to HT?

> The auction is an
> open process, open to all players.

But, as you said, most other players won't get involved. You'll get
mad, but you'll bid as high as it takes to keep your vampire, since you
need minions to play the game.

> If someone thinks the current bid is too
> low, then they can just bid higher. If they lose their vampire, then they
> gain pool which allows them to bring out other vampires,

...which takes time, during which time you may be ousted already or have
that pool taken from you already.

> As LSJ consistently points out, _wrong_ is simply a matter of opinion.
> Personally, I can't see anything wrong with the card at all.

IMO, a card which allows you to take someone else's vampire is wrong.

> Are you suggesting that just because people like to play a particular card
> then it should be changed? Now there's some warped logic.

_I'm_ suggesting that people like to play with overpowered card because
they make you win. But overpowered cards are not really good for the
game. I will be the first one to admit that I think HT is on the
borderline. I challenge anyone on this group to build a deck which
breaks the hell out of HT, post it and let us know how it works.

James

writes

>> So why was Tomb changed, just Sudden Reversal it.
>> So why was Return to Innocence changed, just Direct Intervention it.
>> So why was Fame changed, just Sudden Reversal it.
>> So why was Thoughts Betrayed changed, just Direct Intervention it.
>> So why was Golconda changed, just Sudden Reversal it.
>> I think you get the idea.
>
>In that case, why not just change every master card in the game that looks
>remotely useful. Then you won't have to worry about ever playing Sudden
>Reversal again. It looks like you're implying that any card that is worth
>playing a Sudden Reversal on should be changed.

That's not what was being said at all. All they're saying is that a lot
of people turn round and say "Sudden Reversal" if you have a powerful
master. All that was being pointed out is that Sudden Reversal is not
the be all and end all.

Taking a card which said "Master. 0 pool. Oust your prey." The fact
that you could SR it would not be sufficient to temper its ability and
so it would be broken. Going down the sliding scale, cards such as TOR
COULD be SRed but they can still be very abusive anyway, even with the
threat of SR. Basically, unless you play it on the first two turns of
the game, you automatically get blood onto a vampire equal to the cost
of the card which can be transferred back (assuming you use all your
transfers and you'd be mad not to) and probably a profit (fourth turn or
later).

Other cards have strategies and multiple cards used to get around them.
Strike: Combat Ends.... well, Errata-ed Thoughts Betrayed, Psyche,
Hidden Lurker, Fast Reactions, Dog Pack, Immortal Grapple can all be
used to get round Strike: Combat Ends. You're not stuck to using ONE
card before it becomes abusive.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
James Hamblin wrote:
> Actually, I would say that Hostile Takeover is borderline broken by my
> definition.
> By (2) the card is broken since it requires either a Sudden Reversal, or
> a large expenditure of pool. By (3) the card is broken because it takes
> away your vampire, thus reducing your ability to play the game.

Every player in the game can bid - and you start off by losing
a pool (and spending a Master phase action). How is this broken?
You are on equal footing with all of the other players, except
that you start by losing a pool.

If the original controller can't keep pace with the bid, what's
stopping the other players? And, if one of them gets the vampire,
the original controller *still* gets the pool, and you're *still*
out a pool and a master card action.

Now, if you have that much more pool than each of the other
players, you're winning. Hostile Takeover doesn't change that
state, it merely allows you to take advantage of your previous
good playing.

>Heh. I'm so proud...

>> "bro'ken (adj) : 1. Any card which costs less than, or has a more potent
>> effect than other comparable cards. 2. Any _single_ card which requires
>> concerted efforts from other players to thwart. 3. Any card which
>> prevents other players from playing the game."

[snip]

>Actually, I would say that Hostile Takeover is borderline broken by my
>definition.
>By (2) the card is broken since it requires either a Sudden Reversal, or
>a large expenditure of pool. By (3) the card is broken because it takes
>away your vampire, thus reducing your ability to play the game.

But these arguments also apply to Vulnerability, except that Sudden
Reversal is the *only* defense. Surely Vulnerability is not
'borderline broken'?

I feel that both analyses are failing to take into account the concept of
'opportunity cost.' The opportunity cost of successfully playing
Hostile Takeover or Temptation of Greater Power is huge -- effectively
10 or so *disposable* pool are a requirement. And, to paraphrase,
'some folks might *have* 10 pool, but no one's got 10 pool *to spare*, if
you know what i mean.' It's non-negligible, even with Minion Tap/5th
or some such. There are definitely games where 10 pool are better to
have than a given 10cap vampire; the judgement required to successfully
time the play of HT/TGP, add to its already high opportunity cost.

This high opportunity cost is certainly in the same range as Vulnerability's
(vampire in torpor).

gomi

Messages.Author: Forrest Nielsen
Messages.Body:
I may be misunderstanding this post and discussion, but Tomb of Ramses,
does not get counters. Rather it gives the uncontrolled vampire blood
from the blood bank equivilant to the blood transfers you make from your
pool. Thus there is no such thing as "tomb counters" and the tomb never
has counters on it, rather the uncontrolled vampire gets blood. so if
the tomb is stolen or burned, all counters that were given to the
vampire via the tomb remain on the vampire.
